harness.topology: k6, API and MySQL all on one macOS host; load average during the final runs was 3.76/7.04/7.44
harness.caveat: These are comparative numbers between two architectures on identical hardware, not capacity figures for either.
harness.workload: constant-arrival-rate POST /products; every 4 consecutive iterations share one Idempotency-Key, simulating a double-clicked submit

designA_rejectInFlight.description: First implementation. The leader claims the key in its own committed transaction; concurrent duplicates are answered immediately with 409 REQUEST_IN_FLIGHT and the client is expected to retry.

saturationSweep.note: 20s per step. created always equalled the unique-key count and unexpected stayed at 0 at every rate, including past the saturation knee.

designA_rejectInFlight.tradeoff: Lowest and most stable tail latency measured, but every client must implement retry-on-409.

designB_coalescing.description: Current implementation. Duplicates become waiters that poll the leader's row and return its recorded response, so 409 is gone from the API contract entirely and every caller gets an ordinary success.

defectFoundAndFixed.symptom: 5813 product rows against 5785 idempotency keys — 28 duplicate products, exactly matching 28 lock steals.
defectFoundAndFixed.rootCause: A lease can only show that a leader stopped renewing, never that it stopped working. A merely slow leader had its key stolen while its INSERT was still in flight. Fencing the settle stopped the stale leader recording a result but not from committing its row.
defectFoundAndFixed.fix: The operation now runs inside the leader's transaction, and the fenced ownership UPDATE commits atomically with it. A leader that lost its lease matches zero rows and the whole transaction — insert included — rolls back.
defectFoundAndFixed.verification: Zero duplicate rows across every subsequent run and every swept configuration, confirmed by SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT name), plus a dedicated regression test.

pollIntervalSweep.note: 400 rps, 20s per step. Counterintuitive result: polling faster made latency worse. Hundreds of concurrent waiters each issuing a SELECT every few milliseconds saturate the pool and starve the leaders they are waiting on.
pollIntervalSweep.conclusion: A U-curve with its minimum near a 15ms poll. Pool size mattered far less than poll interval.

finalRuns.outlier: Run 2 degraded severely (p99 1543ms, max 22.6s, 3 waiter timeouts) and has not been root-caused. It is reported, not excluded, and no headline claim rests on the clean runs alone.
finalRuns.correctness: All six runs: rows created exactly equalled unique idempotency keys, and COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT name) was 0. ~142,700 requests in total produced zero duplicate products, including during the degraded run.

legacyBaseline.target: pre-revamp backend/server.js, verbatim except one added `port` config line
legacyBaseline.reproducible: Every run: 75.0% of requests (18000/24001) returned 500 Internal Server Error for an insert whose product had in fact been created. The caller cannot distinguish a duplicate from an outage, so retrying is unsafe.
legacyBaseline.notReproducible: Run 1 only: 328.66 rps, 12.9s max latency, 86 responses with no HTTP status, and 21 unique products never created. Three later runs showed none of it. Treated as a cold-start artifact and excluded from every headline claim.

duplicateRowsUnderConcurrentResubmits.legacy: primary-key violation surfaced as an opaque 500

headline.honestTradeoff: Coalescing removed 409 from the client contract at a measured cost of roughly 3-9x p99 versus rejecting in-flight duplicates, and with noticeably wider run-to-run variance. Correctness was identical in both designs; only the client contract and the tail differ.
